utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Please be seated. And good morning, everybody. Could you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning. This is Case Number IT-97-24-T, the Prosecutor versus Milomir Stakic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. The appearances, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Nicholas Koumjian, assisted by Ruth Karper for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Good to see you again. And for the Defence?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Branko Lukic for the Defence this morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. We had several changes, but no other change: We start with Witness 28 today?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Yes, but we did do a translation. I don't know if Your Honour is referring to that. He gave us a statement yesterday, two pages he wrote out, and there's a draft translation available to the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: To be honest, I don't want to waste time with this. We have to discuss the issue of disclosing material to the Bench at an earlier point in time. This seems to be inevitable. But we are prepared, if the Defence is prepared to work on this basis, we can continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We are ready, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Okay. Then let's -- the witness, to be on the safe side, which kind of protection.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: I rechecked with him this morning, and he is requesting no protective measures in the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: And that we know before, realistic estimated time?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: I think a full day for direct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: A full day for direct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: He is a difficult witness to estimate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: On the basis of what we only saw by the two pages available for us in preparation, one could think that it will be a little bit difficult. But let's not discuss this now. The witness may be brought in, please. So we are in open session, and only may it be possible that we have to go in private session the one or other time, that we can do it in one period.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Off the top of my head, I cannot think of any issue that will require private session. But it could come up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Karagic. Can you hear me in a language you understand?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: And would you please be so kind and read the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. Please be seated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: And may we start with the examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Karagic. Can you please tell the Court, just for the record again, your name.

utterances.speaker: NERMIN KARAGIC
utterances.text: My name is Nermin Karagic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Mr. Karagic, are you a Bosniak?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN KARAGIC
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Can you tell us when you were born.

utterances.speaker: NERMIN KARAGIC
utterances.text: 28th of September, 1974.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Mr. Karagic, I want to discuss with you certain events that happened in the spring, late spring, and the summer of 1992. Would it be correct that at that time you were 17 years old?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN KARAGIC
utterances.text: 17 and a half.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: First I'd like you to tell the Judges a little bit about your biography. Where did you grow up?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN KARAGIC
utterances.text: In wintertime, I lived mostly in the town. I worked on the Prijedor market, also in Ljubija. And the rest of the year I would spend at home.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Could you move up a little bit closer to the microphones, because your voice is soft this morning. Thank you. When you say that the "rest of the year," and I guess that means the spring, summer and fall, you lived at home, is that Rizvanovici, one of the villages in the Brdo area?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN KARAGIC
utterances.text: No, the other way around. It was in summertime that I lived in the town, selling fruit and vegetables, and during the winter, I stayed in Rizvanovici.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. In Rizvanovici, did you live with family? Can you tell us -- you don't need to give us their names, but did you live with your parents or any brothers or sisters?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN KARAGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Can you tell us who, how many brothers and sisters lived with you?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN KARAGIC
utterances.text: Two brothers and two sisters.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Did you work with your father?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN KARAGIC
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Mr. Karagic, I want to go to events that happened at the end of May in 1992. And just to orient you to the time I'm talking about, I'm talking about the attack on Hambarine, shelling of Hambarine. Do you recall where you were when you became aware of shelling of Hambarine?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN KARAGIC
utterances.text: I was at home.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: How did you -- tell us what your experience was. How did you become aware that there was an attack on Hambarine, and what happened to you?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN KARAGIC
utterances.text: All I know was that, all of a sudden, there was shooting on the road at the checkpoint.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: How far is Rizvanovici from Hambarine? Let me -- sorry, to clarify my question, how far was your house from Hambarine?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN KARAGIC
utterances.text: Less than 4 kilometres away, perhaps 3.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: You talked about a checkpoint. Was there a checkpoint between Rizvanovici and Tukovi?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN KARAGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Did you ever participate as one of the men guarding the checkpoint?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN KARAGIC
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: How many men would be at the checkpoint and what kind of weapons did you have?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN KARAGIC
utterances.text: Well, there were about ten of us and only one rifle, an M48.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: After the shelling of Hambarine in the next month - let's talk now about June - did you stay at home in your house? Did you sleep there or what did you do?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN KARAGIC
utterances.text: Can you repeat the question, please? I wasn't following.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: It's no problem. Anytime you don't understand or you'd like me to repeat, please feel free to do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Could I ask the usher to lower the ELMO. And I think Mr. Karagic, it might be a little more natural for you to look at me when I ask the questions. Just have a normal conversation like we did yesterday.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yeah, it's much easier.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: In June, after the shelling of Hambarine, did you sleep in your house, or what did you do? Where did you stay at night?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN KARAGIC
utterances.text: After the attack on Hambarine?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: NERMIN KARAGIC
utterances.text: I spent most of the time outside the house because I was with the patrol in the village.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Did most of the men sleep outside of their homes, most of the men from Rizvanovici?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN KARAGIC
utterances.text: I don't know. I know that a couple of us went together, went around together and just slept out in the open.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you. That's exactly a very good answer. If you don't know, we appreciate you telling us that. I now want to move into the events in July. In July, did some forces enter Rizvanovici?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN KARAGIC
utterances.text: Yes, after the attack on Hambarine. They used to have very frequent patrols in the village, though there were not -- no major incidents at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Okay. You're now talking about after the attack on Hambarine - and I think you know what I'm talking about - and before the cleansing of Rizvanovici. That's the time you're talking about?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN KARAGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Now, I want to talk about the time that you call the cleansing of Rizvanovici. Can you tell the Judges your experience of what happened during that time?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN KARAGIC
utterances.text: When the checkpoint in Hambarine came under attack, very soon -- shortly after that, an APC opened fire and we could see -- we could hear bullets whizzing above our heads and that is the reason we took shelter, in order to avoid getting hurt. Then a tank arrived and opened fire, fired some 20 shells. After that, I don't know how soon after that, but at any rate, I could see the tank from my house. I could see that it fired.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Do you know what month you're talking about now when you saw the tank?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN KARAGIC
utterances.text: Well, it could have been in early July or late June. I'm not sure. It was long time ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you. So after this tank came and fired the shells -- first let me ask: Did you see what the tank was firing at? Did you see where the shells hit?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN KARAGIC
utterances.text: It was firing at the village, at the mosque, probably in order to create panic amongst the population, although at the time I was not fully aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Was there a mosque in the village of Rizvanovici?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN KARAGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Is that the mosque that you're talking about that was fired upon, or was it a mosque in another village?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN KARAGIC
utterances.text: In Hambarine, it was the Hambarine mosque that was targeted at the time of the attack.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Do you know if the tank shells hit the mosque?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN KARAGIC
utterances.text: I think that they damaged the top of the mosque to a certain extent, and the Rajkovac mosque was also hit.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: What about the mosque in Rizvanovici? There was one there, Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. correct?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN KARAGIC
utterances.text: Yes, there was. But at that time, as I told you, I didn't dare move around the village; I was already hiding. But I don't think anything happened at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Did any soldiers enter Rizvanovici?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN KARAGIC
utterances.text: They would pass through the village in a patrol, in a vehicle. I know that there were cases of looting, but mostly by night. I don't know exactly about everything that was going on at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Okay. And can you explain to us, why is it you didn't know everything that was going on? What were you doing during this period of time?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN KARAGIC
utterances.text: I was working and hiding. Actually, at that time, we were already hiding in a basement. There were people from Hambarine staying with us, including my aunt who lived in Hambarine. So -- well, we knew what was going on, and it was not really a good idea to walk around, although I did go out into the village from time to time, but very rarely.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: When you went out to the village, did you talk to other people about what was going on when you weren't there, what the soldiers were doing?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN KARAGIC
utterances.text: Everybody knew about that, because there were many refugees in our village. They had been there for quite a while before the cleansing started.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: When you talk about your village, Rizvanovici, what was the ethnicity of most of the people that lived there?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN KARAGIC
utterances.text: According to what I know, there was only one Croat living in the village of Rizvanovici; the rest were all Muslim.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: When you talk about refugees, these are refugees of what ethnicity and from what part of Bosnia or of what part of the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN KARAGIC
utterances.text: Before the war started in our area, there had been about 50 refugees from Bosanska Dubica as a result of the war in Croatia. So we were also aware of what was going there. And they were throwing shells at us on purpose to make it look like it was the other side that was shelling us.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Okay. I think -- are you talking about shelling that happened in Bosanska Dubica or Bosanski Novi, somewhere like that?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN KARAGIC
utterances.text: I'm talking about Bosanska Dubica. My grandmother comes from there, so I know that the town was shelled. They wanted to make it look like it was the Croats who were shelling them, but it was actually them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Okay. These refugees, then, from Bosanska Dubica, what ethnicity were they?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN KARAGIC
utterances.text: Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Okay. During the month of -- so during this time period when you were hiding and the patrols were coming through, did you see any damage or injuries or deaths, dead bodies, that were caused by the soldiers?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN KARAGIC
utterances.text: I'm afraid I didn't understand your question. I was actually thinking of other things.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: No problem. During the time that you were hiding around the town, did you see any dead bodies, first of all?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN KARAGIC
utterances.text: No, not at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Did you hear from other people about any deaths or arrests that were taking place, any killings or arrests that took place?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN KARAGIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I heard about a bus who was travelling to Dubica. Some people were taken off that bus and killed. And I also heard stories about what happened after the attack on Hambarine. I knew that there were casualties already, though personally I didn't see any.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Did you talk to somebody named Kadiric from Rizvanovici about what happened in his part of the village?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN KARAGIC
utterances.text: I don't know. It's possible. I talked to everyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: I want to move on. At one point, did you and a group of people go to the woods and talk about what you would do?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN KARAGIC
utterances.text: No. I personally -- I was personally hiding out in the field, I mean before the cleansing but also sometime after the cleansing. But at one point in time, we went to the free territory.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: You went to the free territory or you decided to try to go to the free territory?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN KARAGIC
utterances.text: Yes, after the cleansing, we decided to go there, but unfortunately didn't manage.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: When you say that you decided, who was it -- how many people were there that talked about going to the free territory?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN KARAGIC
utterances.text: I didn't make the decision at all. Simply, a man arrived - this man was a neighbour of mine - and he told us who were hiding in that place, that they had decided to set out in the direction of Bihac toward the free territory. And then we joined them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. That's much clearer. Can you tell us, did anyone else from your family go with you in that attempt to reach Bihac?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN KARAGIC
utterances.text: Yes. My father, my brother, my neighbour. In fact, all of them were my neighbours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: How many people do you think there were altogether that set out for Bihac?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN KARAGIC
utterances.text: In total, I estimate that there may have been 300 or more people.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Was this a group that was planning on travelling with vehicles or were you planning on all travelling on foot to reach Bihac?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN KARAGIC
utterances.text: We set out on foot.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: In the group, was it all adult men or men, let's say your age, 17 and over, or were there any women and children?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN KARAGIC
utterances.text: I didn't see any women. There were some children because, later on, there were children who were taken prisoner together with me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: In that group of 300 or so people, do you know -- did you see any weapons at that time or later, after you were captured?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN KARAGIC
utterances.text: Then I saw a few rifles, and I saw them later on as well. When we were captured, there were four or five rifles in the group, or maybe nine.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: What happened as the group started to walk to Bihac? I'm sorry, let me back up a moment. Was this group travelling on the roads? Were you travelling openly or were you trying to travel hiding yourselves?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN KARAGIC
utterances.text: Well, when I think about it, when I think of my experience, it seems silly. We went through woods but also over the open hills, so that everyone could see us.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: What happened to the group when you were walking?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN KARAGIC
utterances.text: We were resting in a village called Kalajevo, or rather it was a wood called Kalajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Is this in the municipality of Prijedor, the woods?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN KARAGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: What happened then?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN KARAGIC
utterances.text: As we were resting, there was a creek there, and we heard shooting and shouting, "Stop, stop, don't run." And there was shooting so we started to run. We started to flee.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Go ahead. And what happened after that, after the group started to flee? Did you all go in one direction together, or did the group break apart?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN KARAGIC
utterances.text: The group broke apart.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: What happened then?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN KARAGIC
utterances.text: I joined a group, and as we were running, I asked, "Where's my father?" So I joined that group. I think that was the bigger group.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Was your brother in that group also?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN KARAGIC
utterances.text: No. My brother went off somewhere else.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: What happened to the group that you and your father were in?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN KARAGIC
utterances.text: We ran for a long time and then we ran into a wood, and we heard shouting, saying, "You are surrounded, surrender." And then I saw people hiding four rifles under the leaves and the people putting their hands up and going out one by one.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Did you see the group, the people that were telling you to stop and that had earlier been shooting at you? Can you tell us who they were? Not their names, but were they army, were they police?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN KARAGIC
utterances.text: I was not able to see them until they lined us up in a column because I was at the end of the column.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Okay. So after you had to come out with your hands up, then what happened? Did they line you up at that point?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN KARAGIC
utterances.text: Yes. They lined us up in four lines and they counted us. There were 117 of us.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: The people that you just called "they," the ones who were counting you, tell us who they were. Were they men in uniform?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN KARAGIC
utterances.text: Yes, they were. They were in JNA and reserve police uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: After they lined you up in four rows, what happened?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN KARAGIC
utterances.text: They told us to empty our pockets and to throw everything on the ground: our money, our watches, our documents. And then they fired shots in the air to frighten us while another one went from one of us to the other, searching us. He had a small pistol. There was a man who had a small pistol and who threw it down on the ground with the other things, and they threatened to cut his throat.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: What happened to all the things that you had thrown out from your pockets, and the watches?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN KARAGIC
utterances.text: I'm not sure because, later on, when we were in the dom, we also had to take off watches and give them to them. So I was surprised by that. I don't know if some people managed to keep their watches at that point.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Okay. After they had searched the 117 people in your group, what happened?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN KARAGIC
utterances.text: Then they lined us up in one column and led us to the road so that a vehicle could come and pick us up.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: How many vehicles arrived, if you remember?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN KARAGIC
utterances.text: I know only about one van which came to pick us up several times.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Where were you taken?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN KARAGIC
utterances.text: We were taken to Miska Glava. When we were passing by the woods, three men tried to escape. They shot one. The others managed to escape but they were killed later. I heard that from a colleague. They were killed in the area of Sanski Most.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: So now there's 114 of you, if my math is correct. And you said you were taken to Miska Glava dom. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN KARAGIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: I don't think we got your answer. Is that yes, that's Miska Glava dom?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN KARAGIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, it said on it "Serbian Bosnia and Herzegovina cultural club, Miska Glava." That's what it said.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Can you tell the Judges, what kind of place was that? Do you know what it was --

utterances.speaker: NERMIN KARAGIC
utterances.text: It's a village.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: What village was it in?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN KARAGIC
utterances.text: You mean Miska Glava?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Yes. And what was the building used for before? Was it a gymnasium, was it a school, was it offices?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN KARAGIC
utterances.text: I think that's how it was with us, the secretary of the local commune had his offices there. Meetings were held there, meetings of the local commune, and there were events. That's how it was in our village, Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. so probably the same happened in that village also.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: So it was common in the former Yugoslavia or at least in Bosnia to have cultural centres in towns and villages called "dom" that the community could have meetings in and various events. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN KARAGIC
utterances.text: Yes, at least in my part of the country. I was younger, I didn't go elsewhere. But in a few villages in the Brdo area, yes, that was the system.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Perhaps we could put a map on. This map, I don't believe is marked yet. It has the title over it of "Ljubija Brisevo overview" and the ERN number of 01248889.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Can we please hear what is the next "S" number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Therefore, provisional S169.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Mr. Karagic, if you could look on your right at the map that's on the screen. Instead of looking at the screen, I'd like you to look at the map itself. And perhaps you can take something to point with. I just ask you to look now at the map. Do you recognise the areas that are depicted on this map, Prijedor, Tukovi, Ljubija, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN KARAGIC
utterances.text: Well, the map is not complete. But yes, I do recognise the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Do you know about where the Miska Glava would be on this map?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN KARAGIC
utterances.text: I think it should be here.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Okay. Indicating the upper left of the map below the Prijedor/Bosanski Novi boundary, northwest of Ljubija. Okay. Thank you. You can turn away from that for now. What happened when you got to the dom?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN KARAGIC
utterances.text: They locked us up in the cafe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Can you describe the cafe? How big was it? Maybe you could point to some -- this room. Was it bigger than this room or smaller than this room?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN KARAGIC
utterances.text: I think it was about half the size of this room, the cafe there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: How many people were put into that room?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: And if I could just suggest, Your Honour, perhaps at some time we could put in the dimensions of this room into the record, since I've asked several witnesses to refer to it. I don't know if anyone has measured it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Let's try. And, of course, this brings me to the point, when you bring in a map, it would be better if a scale would be indicated. Sometimes it's difficult to understand. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: How long did you spend in that room in the dom? How many days and how many nights?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN KARAGIC
utterances.text: Two nights, three days.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: When you got to the dom, at any time was -- did anyone take your personal information or were there any lists made of the people, the 114 people, who were with you?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN KARAGIC
utterances.text: Yes. They listed all our names and dates of birth, and even where each person came from.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: How did they do that? Did they just ask you for that information, or did they check identifications? Did they check cards that people had?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN KARAGIC
utterances.text: I don't know. I couldn't follow what was going on outside, but the list was outside and then they took people according to the list.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Did you have an identification card, and if not, why not?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN KARAGIC
utterances.text: I didn't. I wasn't old enough to have one. Or I may have had the right to it, but I doubt it because you had to be 18. You had to be of age to have one.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Can you help the Judges to understand what the conditions were like in that dom for those -- that time period. First, can you tell us how much food did you receive during the time you were kept in the dom?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN KARAGIC
utterances.text: In those three days, they threw a single loaf of bread in for us to share, and a packet of sweets.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: For all 114 men to share?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN KARAGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Who was guarding the dom? Were there people in uniforms? Could you tell who they were or what units they were from?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN KARAGIC
utterances.text: I think it was the Miska Glava Territorial Defence, and they were wearing JNA uniforms. I didn't see any other kind of uniforms in that place, although at the place where we were taken prisoner, there were also reserve police uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Just so that we're clear, when you say a JNA uniform, can you describe it, what colour it is, and is it a solid colour or camouflage?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN KARAGIC
utterances.text: A solid colour, olive-grey. That's what we called those uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: What about the reserve police uniforms that you talked about? Can you describe those?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN KARAGIC
utterances.text: Their uniforms seemed to be winter uniforms. They were made of a heavier cloth than the other uniforms and it was easy to distinguish them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Was it the same -- were they the same colour, olive-grey solid, or were they a different colour?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN KARAGIC
utterances.text: They were bluish.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: In the dom, can you tell us, did you get as much water as you wanted to drink?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN KARAGIC
utterances.text: It was summertime. The room, as I said, was half the size of this room, and perhaps even -- I think it was even smaller, perhaps. So that inside, I can't describe the heat. And we were so thirsty. They did give us water, but we had to earn it. We had to sing -- we had to sing songs about Greater Serbia. Had they pissed in it, we would have drunk it. We were so thirsty.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Did you ever see anyone urinate in the water that you were given?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN KARAGIC
utterances.text: I didn't, but I assume they did. But I said this in a theoretical way. Had they done this, we would still have drunk it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Was anyone ever taken out of the room during the time that you were there?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN KARAGIC
utterances.text: They were taking people out all the time and beating them. They would take someone upstairs, and we would hear banging, and they would come back covered in blood, and then they would take someone else. And I remember best when my father was taken outside. He was beaten outside the building, and I could hear his moaning. When he came back, he showed me what they had done. He pulled his shirt up and it was all -- his skin was all black and blue. I asked him: "Father, what should I say if they take me outside? What shall I tell them?" I said -- he said: "Son, tell them everything you know." But they didn't take me outside.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: When they chose people to go outside, did they call them by name or did they just come in the room and pick someone by sight?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN KARAGIC
utterances.text: For a time, they called out people by name. And then a man arrived who said only: "I need a volunteer." And he would point a finger at someone. He would say: "You, come out," and whoever went out never came back.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Do you know how many people disappeared like that from the dom while you were there?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN KARAGIC
utterances.text: Ten men were taken by a man whose son was allegedly killed in Rizvanovici, and a man from Cazin and another from Visegrad, so that he alone took 12 men, not counting the one who called them out one by one. He -- that one killed at least three.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Now I want to perhaps go into what you just mentioned and discuss that in a little more detail. You said a man came whose son was allegedly killed in Rizvanovici. Did he or someone else tell you that his son had been killed in Rizvanovici?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN KARAGIC
utterances.text: No, he didn't say that. He just said he wanted ten volunteers from Rizvanovici to go out. But the other man standing at the door, the one who took people out one by one, was talking to someone else at the door. And he said that the Muslims had slaughtered this man's son, gouged his eyes out, cut off his ears, and that he would do the same to the men he was taking away.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Just so we're clear which persons we're talking about, the man who took out, you said, at least three men one by one, can you describe how he would dress? How would he dress? Was he in uniform? Did he have any hat or gloves that you remember?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN KARAGIC
utterances.text: Yes. He had an olive-grey uniform. He was present when we were taken prisoner, and then he had an ammunition belt with him. But later on, he just had a knife, and he wore black gloves. And when he took out a man, he would come back, and his knife and some of the fingers of the glove would be blood-stained.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Okay. Just so we're clear, when you talk about that man, we'll talk about the man with black gloves so we know which one we're talking about. Now the other man that you said came and asked for ten volunteers from Rizvanovici, whose son you heard had been killed in Rizvanovici, was he in uniform or civilian clothes?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN KARAGIC
utterances.text: I don't know. I couldn't see. Maybe I did see him, but I forgot later.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Okay. When he asked for ten volunteers from Rizvanovici, or someone asked for that, what did you do?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN KARAGIC
utterances.text: I got up when they did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Do you know? Can you explain to us why you got up?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN KARAGIC
utterances.text: Well, because of everything. Simply, it was worse watching all this than being killed because it's always possible that your turn will come, so it's better to get it over with.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: What happened after you stood up?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN KARAGIC
utterances.text: I was perhaps the seventh or the eighth. At that moment, I was looking through the window. I was standing right next to the door, and I watched Islam Hopovac being beaten. He kept turning around as a bicycle wheel. And later, when he was brought back, he was all black and blue. We could see that he had suffered a concussion.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Who was Islam Hopovac? Did you know him from somewhere?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN KARAGIC
utterances.text: He was the brother of my sister-in-law.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: The people that were in your group, were they all Muslims, to your knowledge, or were there other ethnicities in the group?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN KARAGIC
utterances.text: They were all Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: So you were standing up and you saw Islam Hopovac being beaten. And what happened then?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN KARAGIC
utterances.text: I was ordered to sit down, and that is what saved my life, the fact that they shouted at me. But when the other ten, including these two men from Cazin and Visegrad went out, the doors closed, and we could hear that one of them was actually being killed right outside the door. We could hear his cries, and it sounded as if his head was being squashed. The sound was very strange, like two pieces of metal pushed against each other, plus the moans and the cries.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Do you know why -- first, who ordered you to sit down?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN KARAGIC
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't know. I just heard someone shout out "sit down" and I sat down. But I think it was a young man who yelled at us and told us to sit down. He could have been 22 years of age, perhaps a bit more. I don't know. He could have been my age now.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Did the ten men -- ten other men, did they go out of the room, all Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. ten of them? There was a group that had been asked to volunteer from Rizvanovici. You said that they had asked for ten volunteers. How many men actually went out of the room at that time?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN KARAGIC
utterances.text: Twelve. One was from Cazin and one was from Visegrad. He had been with us as a refugee. His father and his son were also there. Well, I don't know this was his son or his son-in-law but, at any rate, he was the one who went out instead of him.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Did those people, dozen or so people, ever return?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN KARAGIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Just briefly, in that space in the room where you were, did you have enough room to lie down, all of you?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN KARAGIC
utterances.text: We stood on the tile floor. We were crouching. It's difficult for me to show it to you now. And we were cramped next to each other.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: I can understand it's difficult to show it sitting down. So if you would like, you can step up and just show us how you sat. Just do that now. Take your headphones off.

utterances.speaker: NERMIN KARAGIC
utterances.text: Okay. I'm not going to take them off. This is the position that we were in.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Indicating with knees to chest, and arms around the legs. Thank you. What happened when you left the dom? How did it happen that you were taken away?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN KARAGIC
utterances.text: There was shelling going on in the vicinity, and they panicked. They shouted out to each other: "Let's go fight." But some of them didn't dare. At any rate, two buses came at that point to fetch us, and they put us on to these two buses. What happened with the fighting, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: So all of you that remained alive in that room were put on the two buses?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN KARAGIC
utterances.text: Yes. I brought in Islam Hopovac. And before we left, two of the people from our group went out to bury one dead body. But I don't know exactly where they buried it or who it was that was buried. These two men are both dead now.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Did those two men who went out to bury the body -- was this a body near the dom? Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: NERMIN KARAGIC
utterances.text: They came back very quickly. I didn't see who or what, but I know that the chest of one of them seemed torn open. That's what they said. And they buried him.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you. And the two men who buried the body, did they get back on the bus with the rest of you?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN KARAGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Where did the two buses go?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN KARAGIC
utterances.text: We went to Ljubija.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Did you pass through the town?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN KARAGIC
utterances.text: Yes, we did, through the centre of Ljubija.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: What did you see when you were passing through Ljubija?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN KARAGIC
utterances.text: There were many soldiers there. The 6th Krajina Brigade was there. They were wearing camouflage uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: On your buses, on the bus that you were on, did you see any soldiers or police escorting you?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN KARAGIC
utterances.text: No. We had to keep our heads bent down and -- but I managed to take a peek and that's how I saw it. But I couldn't actually observe what was going on. I only know that the streets were teeming with soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: After you passed through Ljubija, where did the buses go?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN KARAGIC
utterances.text: We went to the stadium which is located between Donja and Gornja Ljubija.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: I'd like you to turn back to the map that's on your right. Do you see in there, in the map, Donja or D. Ljubija and Ljubija?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN KARAGIC
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: And is that the area that you're talking about, between Donja Ljubija and the main part of Ljubija?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN KARAGIC
utterances.text: It would have been here, most probably -- I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Can you push the map, then, slightly to the right. Hold on. The usher will help. I'd like you now to look at the pictures and tell me if you recognise any of the photographs.

utterances.speaker: NERMIN KARAGIC
utterances.text: This is the area where we were taken. Here is the stadium. This is where we were.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you. The witness pointed to photograph number 2, for the record.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: When you say that's the stadium, it's hard for us to really see the stadium. Where is the playing field? Is it behind that fence that we see?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN KARAGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: There's a white, looks like a two-storey building, white on the top and cement on the bottom. Is that part of the stadium?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN KARAGIC
utterances.text: I cannot tell whether the fence was behind or in front of this building, but at any rate, the building served as the changing room for the athletes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: When you talk about what's going to happen, I think you're going to refer to a wall. Is the wall that you're going to be speaking about in this photograph, or part of it?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN KARAGIC
utterances.text: Yes. One can see a wall, a brick wall here, but it is a very long wall so you cannot really see all of it. It is as long as the stadium.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: And is the wall the -- in this picture, it begins where the stream -- along the stream?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN KARAGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. I'm done with that for now. What happened when the buses arrived at the stadium?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN KARAGIC
utterances.text: We were ordered to get off the bus. The bus driver was standing at the entrance to the stadium, and we were made to run. As we passed by him, he hit us. He dealt us each a blow. So we actually had to run into the stadium and line up against the wall.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm beginning now an area that may take some time. Maybe I could finish it in 15 or 20 minutes, but I'm not sure. But I do not want to interrupt it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I understand. And we should have a break as soon as possible. I have got the impression that you, Mr. Karagic, have already got good contact to Mr. Koumjian. Is it the first time you're in a courtroom ever, today?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. No. You know, it's about my personal experience, what I personally experienced, so it's not a problem for me to tell about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: You only should know, I didn't introduce in the beginning who is here. If I would be in your position, I would feel totally uncomfortable in a room with people one doesn't know and then tell about the own experiences. Therefore, I should introduce. You know already Mr. Koumjian. He has two assistants preparing the case. Here in front of the Judges, you have an usher. The lady before me is assisting the Judges, and the lady sitting here is working for the registry, taking care of all our paperwork and so on. And there you have Dr. Stakic, the Defence counsel; and the three Judges from Morocco, from Ukraine, and from Germany. And we are all human beings and, please, don't be afraid. We are doing our work as human beings, as you are a human being. And so it's necessary that, by tradition, that we have our gowns. It's only to show that we are sitting here not in our private capacity but doing our work as counsel, Judges, or in the other functions. Therefore, you shouldn't be afraid when we restart. We have a break now, and feel comfortable. I know it's very difficult for you to give the testimony here but you shouldn't be afraid about the persons here in the room. If you have any other questions --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I trust you. Well, I'm actually glad that the gentleman over there can see me. But I'm sorry that he should have done that -- at least, these people I'm talking about. I don't know about him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Let's have a break of half an hour. That means we stay adjourned until 10.45.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Please be seated.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: May I proceed, Mr. President?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Mr. Karagic, when we -- before the break, you mentioned that the prisoners all had to run out of the bus and line up along the wall. Was that the prisoners from both buses?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN KARAGIC
utterances.text: I don't know. I wasn't paying much attention to that. I know that people from my bus got off. And as we were running, I could see that some of the people had already been lined up against the wall.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: When you lined up against the wall, that's the wall that was in the photograph that you looked at earlier today. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN KARAGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: And how did you stand against the wall? What were the instructions given to you?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN KARAGIC
utterances.text: At that moment, it happened spontaneously. We were lined up in two rows. I don't remember any distinct order to that effect. They may have motioned to the wall. There was this man hitting us, and we were made to run. And we all ran as fast as we could in order to avoid his blows.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: The man hitting you and any of the other guards that were there, can you describe, if you recall, were they wearing uniforms and what kind of uniforms?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN KARAGIC
utterances.text: There was a major there. The one whom I saw later was wearing an olive-grey uniform. A police officer was wearing a camouflage uniform, and he also had a white belt on. Later on, I would see him shooting at a man. I'm not sure about others. I didn't see them clearly. I didn't see their faces. I wasn't paying much attention to that. But they were all wearing uniforms. There was one, though, who was in civilian clothes, a Vojvoda. That's what they called him.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: And Vojvoda, does that mean "duke," and is it a word that was often used among Chetniks for a hero of the Chetnik forces?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN KARAGIC
utterances.text: I don't know. Maybe the gentleman over there could give you a better explanation. It's their custom, after all. He was some kind of leader. It denotes -- the word denotes some kind of leader, hero. The gentleman, if he's willing, I'm sure will give you a better explanation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Would it be correct that the other men that you saw except for this individual wore some kind of uniform, is that correct, the other men with guns?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN KARAGIC
utterances.text: Will you please repeat your question? I missed a detail.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Actually, I think you've already answered it, so I'm going to move on. What happened next? After you were lined up against the wall, tell us what happened?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN KARAGIC
utterances.text: We were ordered to take up this position, to bend down a little Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. bit.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: And for the record, the witness stood up and bent forward at the waist, with his back more or less parallel to the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: After you were put in that position, what happened?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN KARAGIC
utterances.text: Then they started kick us in this area here. At least, that's where I was hit. But there was a stream of blood running along the wall.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: For the record, again, the witness --

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Sir, you indicated you were hit, and you pointed. Did you point to the bridge of your nose, is that correct? Just between the eyes, the nose, at the top.

utterances.speaker: NERMIN KARAGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Do you still have a scar from that?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN KARAGIC
utterances.text: I had one here on the nose. There is a videotape which was taken ten years ago -- excuse me, a photograph taken ten years ago, where you can see the scar much better because later I had a surgery. But at the time, this area here was fractured as a result of the kick. But you can see the scar on this tape.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: So after you were kicked in the nose, what happened then?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN KARAGIC
utterances.text: After that, we stood up. Then a man was brought in, a Croat or a Muslim, whom they had captured in the woods, and they asked me -- asked him to point out those who had been with him in the woods. So he pointed to two or three men in particular, Ismet Avdic, Ermin Kadic -- no, not Ermin Kadic, sorry. Ermin was taken out in another group. Ferid Kadiric or Kadic. That was his surname. His son was also there amongst us and he was also killed. They were singled out and taken to the other side, to the fence. There was a fence next to the wall. And after an individual was pointed out, he would be singled out and taken to the other side, to the fence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Do you know about how many people were taken to the fence?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN KARAGIC
utterances.text: I don't know exactly how many, but the group was almost as large as ours. But I don't know how many there were. I was really frightened. My mind wasn't clear. But I could see that there were a lot of people there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: What happened to those who were taken to the fence, as far as you saw or heard?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN KARAGIC
utterances.text: We were then ordered to look away, towards the wall, which we did. But I managed to glance at the other side and I saw this man wearing a white belt, shooting three bullets into one of the men in this group. He was actually playing with his pistol. He kept turning over the magazine and he shot at the man as he pleased. And then this Vojvoda, this duke, came and he told him not to shoot, not to disturb the neighbourhood. And he said that others would come. In the meantime, those who were younger than me, although I was also a child at the time, were separated and taken to another direction that I pointed out on the photograph.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: They were taken towards the dressing room or another direction?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN KARAGIC
utterances.text: They took them to the dressing room. This is what I learned later from these children when we met subsequently because, at that moment, we were not allowed to watch.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: You mentioned a man with a white belt who shot at some -- one of the prisoners. When you say a white belt, was he wearing a uniform with a white belt or civilian clothes?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN KARAGIC
utterances.text: Yes, he was. But it was a multicoloured uniform, not the same as the other ones. It was already getting dark as he was doing whatever he was doing. He was a member of the military police. I had served in the army, so I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: What happened after -- while you were lined up against the wall? Were the soldiers there asking you any questions or asking for information about anything or anybody?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN KARAGIC
utterances.text: The major - we had to call him "major" if we wanted to address him - asked for Mirza Mujadzic, and he was looking for eminent people, wealthier people, and they were questioning us about this. And I heard my old man being beaten. They were probably asking him for money, asking him where he had hidden money or something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: When you were asked to stand against the wall, were you given any instructions about how to stand against the wall?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN KARAGIC
utterances.text: We had to put our hands on the wall like this. The wall was like this. And I don't know how tall I was at the time, but we had to place our fingers on the top of the wall, and there was a man up there walking over our fingers while we had to sing songs about Greater Serbia. And all this time, they were hitting us from behind. I was hit in the back and I hit my head against the wall. And as you can see in the photograph, the wall was solid brick.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: What happened then? You mentioned that the Vojvoda said not to disturb the neighbourhood with shooting. What happened then after that?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN KARAGIC
utterances.text: He said machines would come. They probably did, because I felt something hit me in the back. It was something soft and heavy, and it hit me so hard I fell down. Then I managed to get up. If I had stayed on the ground, I would probably have been hit again.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: What was happening to the other prisoners at that time as far as you could tell?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN KARAGIC
utterances.text: The other soldiers?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: The other prisoners. What was happening to other people?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN KARAGIC
utterances.text: Oh, the prisoners. They were beaten. We were all beaten. They would go down the line and beat each one in turn. And out of the corner of my eye, I saw a man next to me being killed. There were rifles there as well because, when I carried that man's body later, his head was missing. You could hear him dying, but he was cursing at them like a real hero. I don't know who he was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Was there one prisoner who asked to be taken away from the group, to be separated?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN KARAGIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. He said his mother was a Serb, and they did separate him off. He went there to the changing rooms. I forgot to mention it. And he's still alive. He's living abroad.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: What happened then at the wall during -- after this beating, the beatings that you're talking about?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN KARAGIC
utterances.text: They beat us for several hours. It was already getting dark. There were a lot of people who were dead, whose brains had been spilled out. They started arguing. They wanted to kill us all there, but one of them said: "Well, are you going to carry the bodies?" They didn't want to have to carry the dead bodies away. So we had to collect the bodies.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: So the prisoners that were alive had to pick up the bodies of those who were dead. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN KARAGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Did you pick up any bodies?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN KARAGIC
utterances.text: Yes, two of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Where were the bodies taken?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN KARAGIC
utterances.text: To the bus, to the empty part of the bus where there were no chairs. It was in the back of the bus. I don't know if there are buses like that here.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Do you know if there was one bus or two buses, or how many buses are you talking about?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN KARAGIC
utterances.text: I'm sure there was one, so there was at least one. But I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. When you placed the bodies on the bus, can you describe in any way or estimate in any way, help us estimate, how many bodies there were that were put on the bus?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN KARAGIC
utterances.text: When I was carrying the second body in, the first one did not have a head, as I said. The second one had his eye hanging out and his head had been smashed in, probably with a bayonet or a crowbar. Then I sat on a wooden seat in the back of the bus. And although I was terrified, I looked, and I saw a pile. I don't know, it was perhaps a metre high. The sides of the bus were packed with dead bodies, I think maybe 15 or 20 of them, but I can only guess how many there were. I didn't count them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: The two bodies that you carried, did you think you might have recognised one of them?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN KARAGIC
utterances.text: The first one whose head was missing, I knew who he was but I didn't know his name. I mean, the one without his head. The one that had no head, I thought was my father - although my arms were stiff - he had a pullover on and only half his skull. But when my father was exhumed, his head had been smashed in. But this might have been someone else. I can't be sure whether that was my father or not. But later on, when he was identified, that's how it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Are you sure that your father was on the bus to the stadium?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN KARAGIC
utterances.text: When we were arriving at the stadium?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: NERMIN KARAGIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes. Just before that, they had called our names out and said: "Are there any members of the Karagic family here?" Then he was beaten. The man who asked this kicked him. So I saw my father nodding to me, giving me a signal to keep quiet.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: What was it about the body you carried that made you think it might have been your father at that time? What did you recognise? Was there something in the clothing or the body itself that made you think it might have been your father?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN KARAGIC
utterances.text: He had a pale blue pullover, and in Miska Glava he had the same pullover on. However, it was warm so maybe he gave it to somebody else later on. But the man whose body I carried was approximately the same weight as my father; he was the same build.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Looking back on that now, do you think that was your father? Are you sure? Are you uncertain? And tell us why, if you are uncertain, why you're not certain that was your father.

utterances.speaker: NERMIN KARAGIC
utterances.text: I'm not quite certain because when I sat on the bench in the back of the bus, I looked up toward the front of the bus and I thought I saw my father looking at me. I bowed my head, and after that, I didn't see him any more. I may have been mistaken. I was terrified.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: When you say you bowed your head, was that an instruction that you received or did you do that on your own?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN KARAGIC
utterances.text: It was natural in those circumstances. I don't remember whether it was an order. But I know that a man raised his head in the bus, and they shot him. I heard the shot. I'm not sure whether they shot him in the head, but I did hear a shot.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: What happened after the bus was loaded?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN KARAGIC
utterances.text: They were shouting all sorts of things: "You're going to Kurevo. Now you'll get your independent Bosnia." I don't know. They didn't use the term "mujahedin" at that time, so they called us "Ustasha."

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Where did the bus -- did the bus start moving? Did you go somewhere?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN KARAGIC
utterances.text: How do you mean, go?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Did the bus drive somewhere after you loaded -- after everyone was loaded on the bus, where did you go?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN KARAGIC
utterances.text: Oh. Well, we had to keep our heads down, and it was already dark outside. I think there was moonlight, but we didn't look to see where we were going. We could just feel the bus turning around. And I heard a female voice on the bus. They were telling her to get out. And I'm not Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. sure but I thought she wanted to stay on the bus. And then they made her get out. I don't know what happened to her. But three or four years ago, I passed along that way and I found some bones on the left side of the road. And I think they might be the bones of that woman. On the other hand, she may have been a Serb. She might have got off somewhere else. I can't be sure about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Do you know what kind of bus you were on, whether it had any markings as to the bus company or...

utterances.speaker: NERMIN KARAGIC
utterances.text: It was blue. In Prijedor, we had Autotransport buses. In Ljubija, there were Autoservice buses. It could have been either one or the other. But I think it's more likely to have been Autotransport. But as I say, it could also have been Autoservice because the buses were similar.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Are you certain it was not a military bus? It wasn't in camouflage or olive-grey?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN KARAGIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. I used to travel by bus in the area of Prijedor and I know that the buses were usually that colour. I'm certain it was not a military bus.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Did you recognise the driver of the bus?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN KARAGIC
utterances.text: I think -- you mean by name?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: No, just at that time, as you recall now, if you remember now, did you -- was his face familiar to you?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN KARAGIC
utterances.text: I heard that he was from Volar. I know that he was in Miska Glava, and that he was the one who gave us water but made us sing Serbian songs in order to impress a woman who used to come there. And he was the one who walked over my fingers on top of the wall. He had a moustache, that driver. He was a thin man. I had the impression for a while that it was another man but -- well, I know who it was. It was him.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Do you know what his profession was before the war?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN KARAGIC
utterances.text: I think he was a bus driver, actually. So he was doing his job and having some fun at our expense also.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Where did the bus go?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN KARAGIC
utterances.text: It took us to the place here in this photograph. I think that's it. The terrain looks similar. I think that's it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Which photograph are you talking about, the one that's on the screen now?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN KARAGIC
utterances.text: Yes, the one that's on the screen now.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Indicating photograph number 4.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Why don't you look at the map to your right and tell us if you recognise any of the other photographs. If not, just tell us.

utterances.speaker: NERMIN KARAGIC
utterances.text: This is the place where this crime took place. And --

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you. For the record, the witness has indicated photograph number 6. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Any other photographs that you recognise or that you wish to comment on? Only if you're certain.

utterances.speaker: NERMIN KARAGIC
utterances.text: I would like to comment on this photograph that was just here because this is not the murder spot itself. The murder happened on the other side, about 150 metres further on. I was there with investigators. I didn't think it was here. It was on the other side of the road, but maybe later they put something here.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Okay. Again, the last answer, the witness was referring to photograph number 6.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Do you know -- you said it happened on the other side. Would that be -- what do you mean by "the other side"? The other side of the hill that's in that photograph number 6?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN KARAGIC
utterances.text: 100 or 150 metres from here. This is where the road begins, going towards Ljubija and Rovska. It's a wide road, and I remember it well because that's where I jumped out of the bus. And I remember Kipe and this area. There are even some tyres here that I ran over when I was fleeing.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: If we could have photograph number 6 again, just for a moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Do you know this particular spot, if there was something else that was -- happened there or that you found there? Did you ever go to this particular spot that's in photograph number 6?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN KARAGIC
utterances.text: I came to this place with investigators.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Was that when you went to the exhumation at Redak, Kipe?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN KARAGIC
utterances.text: No, it was long before that. I searched for that place for two days. So many years had passed and I was not familiar with the terrain, but I knew it was somewhere in that area. And when I found those tyres, I was certain that was the place. But we couldn't pinpoint it exactly. And this is probably what somebody else saw and pointed out.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. All right. The buses that you were on -- it was night-time, you said.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: I'm finished. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Where did the buses stop? Or the bus that you were on, where did it stop? Actually, I'm not worried about the photograph. Don't worry about the photograph, Mr. Karagic. Just describe --

utterances.speaker: NERMIN KARAGIC
utterances.text: It depends from what side the road is coming from, this side or that side. But the road is right next to the grave.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. I don't need the photographs now, but just if you can describe in words. The bus stopped. Did it stop on a road? Did it stop in a town? Where was the area?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN KARAGIC
utterances.text: On the road, on the road. That's where it stopped. It stopped on the road.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Was this an area where there were a lot of houses or businesses? Was it a woody area? Describe the area where the bus stopped.

utterances.speaker: NERMIN KARAGIC
utterances.text: It was not a woody area and there were no houses there. I think that it was something to do with a mine, either a place where they disposed of waste or a place where the -- a mine pit. But this was overgrown. But you could see heaps of material there, so that's where they dumped it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: And did you know the name of that place at the time?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN KARAGIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Did you later learn that this place had a name?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN KARAGIC
utterances.text: Later on, I met two men who escaped together with me. They were older than I was. And they knew the place was called Kipe. But that was not its official name; it was just how it was referred to.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Just so that we understand what you're talking about, I'll call that "Kipe," that place. When you got to Kipe, what happened on your bus?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN KARAGIC
utterances.text: It was night-time. The bus stopped after that woman got off. The bus stopped, and they said that three men should volunteer to get off. Some people got off, and they probably unloaded the dead. I didn't watch that. I had my head down and I was waiting to see what would happen next. Then we heard bursts of gunfire, and then they asked people to get off the bus three by three. And that's how it went.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Were you able to see whether the bus that you were on was -- every seat was full? Was it half empty? Were there more people than seats? How occupied, how full, was the bus?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN KARAGIC
utterances.text: There were more people than there were seats. The seats were full and so was the aisle between the rows of seats. It was packed, but I can't be sure how many people there were. And I don't know how many people were in the back.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Do you know how many people that bus would normally sit?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN KARAGIC
utterances.text: Ten or fifty -- I think there were fifty seats.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Did you tell us before, is it correct that you were seated in the back of the bus?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN KARAGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: As the people were getting off the bus three by three, did they go in any order?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN KARAGIC
utterances.text: I don't know because I didn't watch. I was holding my head down, waiting. They were just saying: "The next three." "The next three." Out of the corner of my eye, I glanced through the window and I saw the bearded man saying: "Here's your independent Bosnia" and shooting. Although it was night-time, I could see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Tell us what happened during this process. What happened to you?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN KARAGIC
utterances.text: It went on for a long time, this calling out three by three. And when our turn seemed to be coming, I think I raised my head at that point and I saw that there were only five or six of us left. We were whispering to each other. I didn't really understand what was happening. And then when they said: "The next three," when I got up, I saw that the man taking people off the bus had been knocked down. One of our people had jumped on top of him and was holding him down together with his rifle. And one of the windows was already smashed, or it was missing. It was the window behind the driver's back. So I wanted to take the opportunity and get out of that -- through that window. I saw bullets hitting all around. The first man who jumped out was killed. Then I jumped out and I turned around, and I saw that the man who was holding down the man who had been taking out was being pulled by the legs by a Chetnik. When I jumped out, the guard could not shoot at me because he was changing his clip. And Kipe begins right there by the road, so I ran, and I fell into a hole. And I lay there. It was about fifty or a hundred metres away from them. And I saw two other men running past. And that's all. And then I got up, too, and continued running away. No one shot after me. They didn't see me. I was already far away from them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: You said that you saw two others running past, past you. Do you know who they were?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN KARAGIC
utterances.text: I know who they were, but I wouldn't now, for other reasons.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Were they prisoners from your bus?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN KARAGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: As far as you know, were they part of the last group of five or six people that you talked about that were on the bus?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN KARAGIC
utterances.text: Yes. I think that one of them had even sat next to me on the bus.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Do you know if anyone else from your bus survived?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN KARAGIC
utterances.text: I know, at least according to what he said, there were survivors. Some of the people managed to get up and flee.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Before we go on to talk about other things, did you attend an exhumation near that location, in Kipe, near Kipe?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN KARAGIC
utterances.text: Once I passed by and I could see that the exhumation was going on but I couldn't go there. They probably did not allow access to passersby, so I just continued on my way.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: At some time, did you attend an exhumation in Redak?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN KARAGIC
utterances.text: That's just what I told you. When I wanted to assist, they wouldn't allow me. So I had to leave the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Okay. At some point, did you identify anyone who was exhumed at that location?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN KARAGIC
utterances.text: Yes, a year and-a-half later. The bodies were probably first taken to Visoko, and then from Visoko to Sanski Most where they were kept, the bodies. I mean, what remained of the bodies.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Who did you identify?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN KARAGIC
utterances.text: My father. Islam Hopovac. His wife came and I showed her what I thought was him. And the one whom I had carried whose eye had been out of its socket was also there. I could identify him. I mean, I could see the injuries, the holes, made by the knife or the bayonet. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Islam Hopovac is the same person that you had seen being beaten when you were inside the Miska Glava dom, when you stood up and looked out the window?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN KARAGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: How did you recognise your father?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN KARAGIC
utterances.text: I found some hair, his hair. He had a similar hair to mine. There was also a piece of his glasses there. He didn't have very good teeth on his lower jaw. And I knew that he had had a number of fractures on his legs before the war. He had had a few traffic accidents. So I could tell that it was him. I even called a lady doctor who was there to explain to her about his previous injuries. So I told her that, and on the basis of that, she was able to help me. And later on, they did a DNA analysis, which also helped, and that is how we established it was him. As for the others, I could tell who they were approximately by their clothes, on the basis of what they were wearing. And I also thought that this could be my father because of the cloth that remained on the body.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Just to be clear, you mentioned the DNA test. Did you give blood, or did anyone else from your family give blood for that test to be conducted?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN KARAGIC
utterances.text: My aunt, she gave blood. I don't remember if I did. I think she was the only one who gave blood, actually. My father's sister, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: And did your family receive the results of that test indicating that it was determined that that was your father?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN KARAGIC
utterances.text: I don't know whether we were given the actual paper but I saw a list which was put up on a board there. The list contained the names of the people in respect of whom a DNA test had been done, and my father's name was also there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Now going back, I want to talk to you about what happened after you escaped the massacre at Kipe. You said you were running and you fell. What happened then?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN KARAGIC
