utterances.text: I kept falling down. I don't know how many times I fell. The area is covered with material which is dumped by these large trucks, and it is a very uneven terrain. I fell in a hole there. I even think that I slept next to this mass grave, but I'm not sure. I know that some dumper truck tyres were there, and I slept next to these tyres. I could see tracer bullets whizzing over my head, but I stood motionless in this area which was overgrown with some shrubbery, and I spent the night there and I woke up the next morning. It is possible that I passed out.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: The next morning after you had slept or passed out and you woke up, what happened then?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN KARAGIC
utterances.text: I think it must have been around 4.00 or half past 4.00. It was at daybreak, at any rate. The night was cool, and I was probably woken by the cold. I passed by this area of Kipe and I passed the truck tyres. And I came up to a small wall which was bordering a little wood there. So I hid there but I was afraid that my shoes were too visible because they were very bright, so I covered them with my hands. Then I took them off, but then I put them on again, and I almost started shouting, "Shoot at me. I cannot stand it any more." I mean, I talked to myself at the time. I thought that the wood was full of them. I thought that there were many people hiding in the area. I was very confused. I continued into the woods, and I started climbing up a hill. And I heard someone shout: "Freeze." And I saw two people in civilian clothes, with no weapons. They were Croats. I don't remember -- I don't think that we introduced each other, that they told me their names. They said that they were from Brisevo. They asked me if I had seen a group of women and children because apparently, a day or two days before, cleansing had taken place in their village. I said I didn't. I didn't see anyone. So we talked for a while about what had happened to us. They showed me the way to Carakovo, and we parted.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Where did you go then?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN KARAGIC
utterances.text: I came to a lake. I don't know which lake it was. I washed myself a little, but my clothes were still covered with blood. There were blood stains on my clothes that I couldn't wash off. After that, I started out along a road, and I ran into an old woman with whom I talked for a while. I picked some fruits there and ate them because I hadn't had any food for days. I asked some people again for the way to Carakovo. It's very easy to get lost in that area. It is a wooded, uneven terrain. And then I also didn't trust people all the time. Eventually, I ended up in the village of Raljas Suljevica.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Did you know where you were going? Did you have an objective in mind?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN KARAGIC
utterances.text: Raljas is the name of the village. Well, my final destination was Carakovo, although I wanted to get to Hambarine. But I thought that I should first go to Carakovo and then, from there, to Hambarine. I spent a lot of time there. I was very careful. I kept crawling through the woods and I spent two days crawling around the area of Raljas. I remember a truck passing by, carrying a group of their men who were singing songs about their Vojvodas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Do you know whether you had any visible injuries on your face at that time?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN KARAGIC
utterances.text: Yes, my face was disfigured. I was covered with blood from the beating that I had sustained before, but also from the falls that happened to me on the way. I still have some problems as a result of those injuries.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: While you were on these journeys, did you ever see or were you aware of any dead bodies in the area that you were walking around?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN KARAGIC
utterances.text: First when I was in Raljas, I was looking for a place which belonged to an old man. I don't know whether this was a mixed village or not. I think that some Croats lived in the area. When I worked in Ljubija, I knew a man by the name of Dragan who lived there, who repaired trucks. So before the war, I had been to Raljas on several occasions, and I was looking for this place. And then I ran into a man who saw me, who saw my face covered with blood. I asked him for some food, but he sent me off to Ljubija. Then I saw a young man wearing what looked like a uniform, sitting outside a house. I don't really know what kind of uniform it was. But at any rate, two days later, I ended up on the other side of Raljas and went in the opposite direction. So on this other end of the village of Raljas, I ran into another Croat. I don't know whether this man is still alive today, but he gave me some food, a piece of bread, some tomatoes. I think he even put some spread on the bread. And he said: "You have to run away. If they see me with you, they will kill me, too." He showed me the way, where to go, and I went in the direction of the village of Vodicno. I actually passed through that village in which I saw a number of dead bodies also. I went up to one of the corpses, but I couldn't approach others because there was this stench coming out of these bodies. I didn't stay there very long. I continued to flee. Most of the time, I had to crawl. But maybe these details are not important. Finally, I reached Rakovcani, where some people gave me some food which I ate, but I also took a loaf of bread with me. I didn't believe that I would find anyone alive there, but there were some people who were still alive in this village. I wanted to cross the road there, but the people who were there were afraid and they told me that I better cross the road further down. On my way there, I saw a woman who told me to -- where to cross the road. I was not -- no longer as prudent and careful as I had been, and I didn't see these men. I didn't see this group of people. There may have been even hundreds of them. I saw this man who was working with cattle. He was trying to tie a cow, and he shouted at me, but I didn't quite realise what he was trying to tell me, whether to come to him or whether to get away. But at any rate, I went up to him and we started to talk. I told him about what had happened to me. It was an old man, maybe 70 years of age. I think he died three or four years ago. I saw this Chetnik on the door, but I pretended I didn't see him. I just changed the subject while still talking to this old man. But he told me to get out. So I got out, and he pointed his rifle at me, at my head. I remember a dog started to bark at him. And then he yelled at the dog, telling it to shut up. But the dog went on barking, and then he killed it. Then he asked me whether I was related to this old man. I think he would have killed him immediately if I had told him that we were related. He asked me about my face because I had these injuries on my face, and I told him that I had fallen down on a rock. Then another one came and they took me outside the community centre in Rakovcani.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Okay. I want to ask you a few questions about what you've told us so far, before we go into what happened after your arrest in Rakovcani. You mentioned when you were passing through Vodicno, that you saw dead bodies. Were these men in uniforms that you saw, the dead bodies, or were they in civilian clothes?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN KARAGIC
utterances.text: Civilians.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Were they all young men or were they -- do you know, or were they of different sexes or ages?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN KARAGIC
utterances.text: I don't know. I went up to one of the corpses. I think that the man was 50 or 60 years of age. Other bodies were stinking, and I didn't want to go there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: You said that if you had told -- that you were asked whether you were related to the old man that you were talking to when you were taken or arrested at Rakovcani. Did you tell him that you were related to the old man, or how did you answer that question?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN KARAGIC
utterances.text: I told him we were not related. I said I didn't even know him, which was actually true. I didn't really know the man, but apparently he knew me because of my grandfather.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: And you said that the man that pointed the gun at you, that arrested you there, was a Chetnik. Can you describe, was he a man in uniform and what kind of uniform?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN KARAGIC
utterances.text: Yes. It was an olive-grey uniform. He had a beard. The other one who came later was wearing a uniform of the reserve police force. I have to leave the courtroom for a second.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: The trial stays adjourned until 12.15. Thank you for telling us. If you need a longer break, please tell us.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, just five minutes will be enough.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Please be seated. Please continue with the examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Sir, I'd like you to look again at the map, if that could be put on the ELMO. You've talked about various things that happened from the Miska Glava dom, and then being taken through Ljubija, through Donja Ljubija to Ljubija, and then Kipe. Can you see on the map where Kipe is? Is that correctly portrayed?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN KARAGIC
utterances.text: Where it says Zune, I think it's somewhere around here, but I'm not sure. I couldn't say. I think -- wait a minute. Here, near Jakarina, here. What does it say here? Lake. It's somewhere around Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. here. It's in this area here.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Sir, that's an English word meaning "lake." Do you see the --

utterances.speaker: NERMIN KARAGIC
utterances.text: Yes, I see. I see.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Do you see the "X" below that, the two "X's"?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN KARAGIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do now, yes. I know that I saw the church here when I was running away. I used it as a point for orientation around Ljubija. It was a Catholic church.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Since you mentioned it, was that church damaged when you saw it?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN KARAGIC
utterances.text: I think it was intact.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: When you went from Kipe, you said you went to some various villages and one of them was Raljas. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN KARAGIC
utterances.text: Raljas is a big area. I may have been in more than one village, but maybe the whole area is called Raljas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Okay. So when you're saying Raljas, you mean a whole area near Ljubija; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN KARAGIC
utterances.text: Every hamlet in the area of Raljas, I call "Raljas," all the houses around here. Until you come down to this place where the built-up area begins, I think it's all called Raljas. I don't know of any other name for it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. I'm done with the map then. And you were telling us before the break that you had arrived in Rakovcani, and that at that point, you had been arrested by a man in uniform with a beard. And what happened after you were arrested?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN KARAGIC
utterances.text: As I've already said, I was taken to the community centre in Rakovcani. He and another reserve policeman, they had me at gunpoint. There was a rifle pointed at my head, and they told me to get in the car. And there were lots of soldiers around. The place was teeming with them. I heard them talking among themselves and mentioning fuel, so then I said: "I have some fuel." Because I thought it might be a chance to escape. So they said: "Get out of the car." And I did. And they put me on a tractor. And one of them pointed a pistol at my head and the other one -- these are little, small narrow lanes. I can't describe it for you because there's nothing like that here. I can't really describe it. The road was maybe 2 and-a-half metres wide and there were houses and low walls on both sides.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: When you told the soldiers that you had fuel, did you tell them where you could find fuel?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN KARAGIC
utterances.text: I didn't tell them then, but we went to my house. I may have said it was at my home. But I know I told them that I had some fuel.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Where you were at that time, at the dom in Rakovcani, how far was that from your house in Rizvanovici?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN KARAGIC
utterances.text: I wasn't inside the dom but outside in the car, near the dom. And the distance was about a kilometre, perhaps.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: What happened then when you went on the tractor?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN KARAGIC
utterances.text: As I have already said, one of them pointed a pistol at my head and drove. The other one who was holding the pistol was wearing a uniform of the reserve police force, and they were afraid of being ambushed. That's how we arrived at my house. In front of the house, there were six or seven thousand bricks, blocks, because we had started building a house, and it's still there, the part that we started building. I think it's 20 metres long and 7 or 8 metres wide. We were going to use that to store fruit and vegetables during the summer, so we dug it 3 metres in the ground. And the bricks I mentioned, I had concealed some fuel there before. But when we arrived there, it was already gone. Somebody else had already found it. So I went to the low wall behind this place where I had a barrel containing 20 liters of fuel. It was a 50-litre barrel but there were about 20 litres of fuel hidden there. I thought I would run away then, but this man had climbed up and was holding his rifle pointed at me so I didn't have a chance to escape. I brought them the barrel and they poured the fuel in.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Then what happened?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN KARAGIC
utterances.text: I wasn't even aware of what I was doing. They poured the fuel out of the barrel, and then they threw it on to the road. And I said to them, as if I was crazy, I said: "Why don't you remove that barrel from the road? It will be in somebody's way." They put me on the tractor again. And we went back to the dom, the community centre in Rizvanovici, in the same way we had come. Their headquarters was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: When you say "their headquarters," did it appear to be a police headquarters or army headquarters, or what kind of group's headquarters?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN KARAGIC
utterances.text: It was the army, but there were reserve policemen among them as well. I think there were more soldiers than policemen. And there was also a school there where they slept.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Was someone introduced to you as the commander?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN KARAGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Tell us about this person.

utterances.speaker: NERMIN KARAGIC
utterances.text: At first, at first when I had just arrived, they started beating me right away. They took their belts off and they started hitting me. They asked me what had happened to my face and I told them that I had escaped from a shooting, from an execution.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: I understood from the answer that they took their belts off. Is that correct? Did they use their own belts, or whose belts did they use?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN KARAGIC
utterances.text: My belt. They took my belt. They took my belt off and they were pulling it, one was pulling each end. And then they hit me from all sides. And one of them lay on top of me and he was pretending to hit me, but I didn't know that then. In fact, he was protecting me so that I would not be badly hurt.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: You made a motion with your hands about the belt, which I understand, but I want to make sure it's clear in the record. What did they do with your belt?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN KARAGIC
utterances.text: They held it to my throat and then they pulled it. They were actually strangling me. And that's how they knocked me down on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Okay. When you said they were both pulling it, were two different soldiers pulling on each end of your belt, with the belt around your neck?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN KARAGIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. They were pulling from behind, at least, that's how I think it was because there were two of them doing this. And they were hitting me from all sides. I think it was the two that took me prisoner who were doing this.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: You mentioned the commander. When did you see or meet the person who you thought was the commander?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN KARAGIC
utterances.text: They were beating me in front of him. He was sitting there, reading a novel, and when they brought me to him and said "hello" and then they started beating me right away. And there were others sitting with the commander, and there were soldiers walking around. I saw a lot of looted vehicles, even my father's car. They were beating me because they wanted to get the car keys.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Did this commander -- or did he tell you what he was the commander of, or did anyone else give you a title for him?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN KARAGIC
utterances.text: He said to me that I had to call him the commander of Serbia, Rakovcani, Biscani, that I had to pronounce this whole sentence enumerating all the villages there. So I had to say that all these villages were Serbian and that's how I had to address him.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: These villages that were part of his title you just mentioned, Rakovcani and Biscani, and whatever others were in the title, were they villages that before the conflict were predominantly Serb?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN KARAGIC
utterances.text: There were never any Serbs there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: After the soldiers were beating you, did the commander show you anything?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN KARAGIC
utterances.text: Show me? First, they took me to have lunch and then he showed me something. I even asked him where he was from, and he told me he was from Banja Luka. I don't know whether he was lying or not, but that's what he said.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Okay. Perhaps it's better if you just tell us what happened. What happened after the beating?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN KARAGIC
utterances.text: The Cafe Bosna was there. It was a nice place where a lot of young people used to gather. They would have dances, and that's where they had their canteen. The commander took me there to question me after the beating. He asked me if I was hungry. And while they were beating me, I had some bread, but they didn't ask me about it. Dropped the bread while they were beating me. I was eating, and there was a soldier to my right, the commander was to my left. And the soldier kept pricking me with his knife in the area of the kidneys, frightening me. The other one was questioning me. And then some identity cards were brought in, a huge pile of them this high. And while he was eating, they kept asking me: "Do you know this one, this one?" And this man was constantly pricking me with his knife, and I was afraid to eat. I said I couldn't eat any more. And then he yelled at me, he said "Eat." And I said: "I can't eat because this man is pricking me with a knife." I could have eaten otherwise. And he said: "You see how the JNA has food, and yet you refuse to serve in the JNA." But I knew that the food actually came from our houses which had been looted. That's why they had so much food.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: The identity cards that were shown to you, did you recognise any of the individuals who were on those cards?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN KARAGIC
utterances.text: I might have recognised most of these people had I not been so terrified, because this man kept pricking me with his knife and I was afraid he would stab me. So I managed to recognise only one, the one who used to work in that cafe. He's the only one I recognised.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: If you remember now, or if you noticed then and remember now, could you tell from the names the ethnicity of the people who were on those identity cards?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN KARAGIC
utterances.text: The last one, the one I recognised, was a Muslim. I wouldn't know about the others. But probably Muslims, maybe Croats, because the Croats had the same problems.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: The commander that you're talking about, can you describe his uniform and whether you recognised any rank on him?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN KARAGIC
utterances.text: It was a JNA uniform. I don't know if he had any rank, insignia. I just had to call him the commander of Serbian Biscani, Rizvanovici and Rakovcani. I don't remember. But I'm sure he was the commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: What happened after you were shown the identity cards?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN KARAGIC
utterances.text: I stopped eating. A soldier came along and offered a cigarette to the commander. So I asked for a cigarette, too. I said: "May I have a cigarette? I haven't smoked in two months." And he gave it to me. I lighted it, and I asked the commander: "Is this my last cigarette? That's how it usually is." And he said: "It's up to you. Will you be our grave digger?" And I said: "Yes, if it meant I would stay alive." And so they found a spade and a pickaxe for me to use and took me behind Smail Karagic's house. Two bodies were there. There were already maggots crawling out of their heads. And there were six others nearby, but I managed to escape in the meantime. But I know there were six other bodies, and there were female bodies among them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Did you bury the two bodies that you're talking about?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN KARAGIC
utterances.text: I dug the grave for them because of the heat. July is the hottest month in our part of the world. I was very thirsty, so thirsty that I Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. even threw my spade down at one point and refused to dig any further. I asked for water, and they yelled at me to go on digging. I again asked for water, and they went on yelling. And I didn't care any more. Well, it's not that I didn't care but I simply couldn't go on. Then they brought me water. I had a drink and continued digging. While I was digging, one of the men who had taken me prisoner shot around my feet and I had to dance, the way people dance in cowboy films. And then I don't know what came over me. I said to him: "Aim at this," and I was talking about the line running down the middle of the spade. And he hit it. And I said: "You're a real good shot." And he laughed at that, and then he fired a whole burst of gunfire at that spade. And then he left, and somebody hit me with a piece of wood. I don't know, I can't remember that precisely. And I was digging again, and this man climbed up a tree and he was cutting some wood to make a stake, about a metre and-a-half long.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Did you actually finish burying the bodies, the two bodies?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN KARAGIC
utterances.text: They told me to put them in the grave and bury them. The grave was knee deep by then. I tried. I pulled one by the feet, but I had the feeling that his feet would come off. So I said I couldn't do it. And he was yelling at me, and I was saying, "I can't." And he fired a shot, and the bullet grazed me. I thought I was dead, so I started to fall down, but there was nothing wrong with me. And then I said something. Then I turned around, and I untied the corpses, because they were bound with strips of plastic. They were bound together. So I untied the plastic and I pulled them into the grave one by one. I buried them. One foot remained sticking out of the soil. In the meantime, the man who had made a stake called to me to come to him. And while I was walking towards him to see what would happen next, I asked him how much my life was worth. He said: "5.000 litres of fuel." And I remembered that my uncle had 200 litres of fuel he had buried. It just passed through my head. And I said: "Well, I have 200." And he said: "Fuck your mother. Why didn't you say that at once?" And then he started to swing the stake at me. I caught hold of one end of the stake and we started tugging at it. I was terrified. I yelled out: "Commander, commander," hoping he would save me. And the commander did arrive. He was holding a knife in his hand. The soldiers lowered their rifles, expecting him to kill me. He was playing with the knife, tossing it from one hand to the other and walking towards me. I dodged. And the grass was not very high. It had been mown about a fortnight before, so there was nothing he could trip over except his own feet, and he did trip. And I took the opportunity and started running away. There was some maize growing nearby and I managed to hide in the corn field so they couldn't shoot at me. And then they threw a grenade. In fact, I didn't know what they were doing, but I heard a whizzing sound and something thudded to the ground. It flew past me but it didn't hit me. And then the grenade exploded, maybe 2 metres away from me. And I had just a piece of shrapnel which hit me in the arm, and my ear was hurt. And there may have been other pieces of shrapnel. But when I had an x-ray taken a while ago, I found that there was a piece of shrapnel still in my arm which I didn't even know about. I ran to the edge of the wood and threw myself into a ditch. They ran past me and went on. They probably weren't expecting me to be there. And I heard them saying: "Well, he's not here. He's not here." And I went in the opposite direction from the direction their voices were coming from, and that's how I managed to escape. I came to an isolated house on the other side of the village near the stream, where I found a piece of cloth and I put it on my ear. I thought it would come off any time. And this is where I spent the night. I actually didn't dare stay in the house because, at one point in time, they noticed me again and opened fire. But I managed to escape once again. And I reached an overgrown area. Luckily, they fired tracer bullets so I could see them. I could see where the shots were coming from, and that's how I managed to escape once again and save myself. I spent the night in the shrubs, some 300 metres away from that house. I woke up the next morning because I was cold. I only had a light shirt on and a pair of shorts. I was freezing. So I removed the branches with which I had covered myself a little in order to warm myself up in the sun. I stay there for a while and then again I set out to -- in a direction of an area between Rakovcani and Rizvanovici. I approached the road and again I hid in a cornfield. I was waiting for the nightfall, to cross the road. Sorry, do these details matter to you? I mean, I don't want to waste your time if this is not necessary.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: I think you have been very helpful to us so far. But from this point, can you tell us in a rather brief fashion now what you did between the time of this escape and when you left on a convoy. Can you describe where you were and what you were doing during that time.

utterances.speaker: NERMIN KARAGIC
utterances.text: Okay, I'll be brief then. I realise you don't need all of these details. As I said, I waited for the nightfall --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: May I interrupt. Please feel free to tell us what you want to tell us and don't have the impression that any detail would be not of our interest. Please, tell us all what you have experienced. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. So I hid in this cornfield which was near the road and waited for the nightfall. I happened to find some tomatoes there, which I ate. Then at one point a truck stopped near the road, and a bullet was fired. And I started to run. I felt as if everybody could see me. I thought I was in a sort of triangle and that they could spot me from all sides. But they couldn't get me, they couldn't hit me. I found a small boundary wall or a hedge, where I hid. There was a slope there, and I took out the cord off my shorts, which I then tied to a tree there. And I tied myself to this tree so that they wouldn't see me. I was hanging upside down, actually, and they were not very far from me. They were like 3 or 4 metres away. They were near me. They stood there but they couldn't see me. And all the while I was holding this knife that I had because I had decided that I would kill myself if they saw me. They were probably looking for me throughout the forest. And this is how I fell asleep -- well, there is a detail here that I don't want to mention. But this is how I fell asleep, and I woke up like this the next morning. It was about 4.00 in the morning. I got out of that spot and I crawled across the cemetery, something which I wouldn't -- I would have never done before. I wouldn't have dared. And I managed to find a hole which my brother and I had dug out a day or two after the cleansing of the village. When I got to this hole, I cried for the first time when I saw that no one was left there. I stayed two days in this hole. I was alone. There were some tomatoes and peppers growing there that we had planted before the war. I picked those and I ate them. And then after two days, I decided to go in the same direction which we had taken that day when we had set out for Bihac. So it was during the second night that I left, and I managed to find a group of 10 or 11 people, including my brother. Two of them had rifles. There were two rifles with this group of people, so that made me feel a bit safer. And we spent the rest of the time together up until the 21st of August, when we joined this convoy. During the night, we would forage for food. And during the day, we hid. They did the other way around. They were out during the day but didn't dare move around during the night.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: When you say, "They did it the other way," do you mean the soldiers, the Serbian soldiers?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN KARAGIC
utterances.text: Yes. They were afraid. They only feel strong when they're together.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: You mentioned when you were hanging in the tree that you had a knife. Where did you get the knife from?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN KARAGIC
utterances.text: I found it in this house, the same house in which I had found this piece of cloth which I used to tie around my ears to keep them from falling off. I didn't actually realise that my ears were all right, but I was afraid because of the blood coming out.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: This was after the injury to your ear from the grenade exploding nearby?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN KARAGIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: During this time that you were back in the Brdo area, I think you indicated that you mainly just moved at night, but did you see any damage to houses in that area?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN KARAGIC
utterances.text: I didn't notice any houses burnt down at the time but later -- actually, it was before that I had seen several houses on fire. But at the time we were in hiding, no, I didn't notice any such thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: When was it that you had seen houses on fire?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN KARAGIC
utterances.text: After the cleansing, a day or two before we left for Bihac. Perhaps five days after the cleansing, I mean throughout that period of time, we saw houses on fire. There would always be a house on fire here and there. That was actually a good sign for us.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Why is that?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN KARAGIC
utterances.text: See, they had this special media campaign which was targeted against us. They were saying that we were the last Turks in the area. They fabricated all kinds of things. I mean, they were lying to their own people, probably including this one sitting here. But this was all a lie. We managed to survive. We were first disarmed. Then they did to us what they did, what they wanted to do with us, but we survived.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Tell us about the convoy in which you left the area.

utterances.speaker: NERMIN KARAGIC
utterances.text: I will. During the time we were hiding, before we joined the convoy, I saw the body of my uncle, though it was difficult to recognise him because there was almost no tissue left on the body. But I knew it was him. This was before the convoy. One day before that, (redacted) had told me about the convoy. I'm not going to tell you his name because of his safety. He told us that a convoy had gone through Travnik and that it had all gone well. So we decided to join it. It was difficult for me to make this decision because of this experience that I had had with them. But eventually, we all decided that we should go. So we joined this convoy and we mixed with a group of women and children on the 21st of August.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Where did you get on the convoy?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN KARAGIC
utterances.text: In Tukovi. It is a village in the immediate vicinity of Rizvanovici, on the outskirts of Prijedor town.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: When you got on the convoy, you said you mixed with women and children. Can you describe exactly what you did?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN KARAGIC
utterances.text: Well, we once again had to go through the cornfield, cross a number of -- cross over a number of farm walls and hedges. It was their area. We tried to avoid them and the road, but we were successful. I was actually surprised to see that they didn't react. There were many of them there, wearing all kinds of uniforms. Some even had -- it's difficult for me to describe it because it was not a usual uniform. It was a kind of windbreaker with dots on it, a very strange kind of uniform. Bluish. The man could have been a military policeman but I'm not sure. Others were wearing the regular JNA uniforms.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: May I please interrupt? Can please line 4 on Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: witness. Thank you. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Did you get on a bus or some kind of -- other kind of vehicle at Tukovi? Can you describe the vehicle?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN KARAGIC
utterances.text: It was a trailer truck. It may have had two trailers but I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: When you got on the truck, did you in any way try to conceal yourself?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN KARAGIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I was with the first group, and I went forward. I was with a woman whose name I don't wish to mention because of her place of work. I mean, it's not important anyway. I sat next to this lady. My brother was at the back of the bus with two other men. And the rest of the passengers were all women.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: So were you sitting in a normal position on the truck?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN KARAGIC
utterances.text: I first sat on the board, on the edge of the trailer. And then someone hit me with a rifle butt and I fell down, and I actually hid down and remained in this position throughout the journey.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: What was hiding you when you were laying down?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN KARAGIC
utterances.text: Well, the women.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: During the convoy, do you know if the escorts, the soldiers or police, ever made any demands on the prisoners, or on the people on the convoy?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN KARAGIC
utterances.text: Well, first of all, I didn't know, I wasn't aware of the fact that there was any escort on the truck. I simply got on to the trailer. And after the truck had set out, my brother shouted out at me, he wanted me to come over to him. He later had problems because of that. I don't know exactly where it was but it could have been in the vicinity of Kozarac. I think that they picked up the people from Trnopolje on the way. We made several stops, many stops, actually, but I don't remember how many. I didn't count them. In the meantime, the driver took my brother off the truck and my brother disappeared for a while. He came back, and he had a stain on his shirt when he came back. I think this driver had pointed his gun at him. Anyway, my brother told me: "I have been ordered, else I would be killed, to tell you that you should give them all the Serbian money because we would not need it in Travnik." Actually, it was the Yugoslav money at the time. So that's how it started. First they asked for the money. Then after the next stop, they asked for German marks, for jewellery, valuables. And whenever they found something on someone, they started threatening us, always through my brother. But anyway, we arrived in a village.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: We didn't get the name of the village.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Anyway, I was not very familiar with the area. These women were crying. They were with children. And they took out a number of people. They took a number of people off the trailer. And this group of people remained behind. Finally, we arrived at Smetovi. And they came up to me and my brother -- actually, a Chetnik came close to us. There were many of them, and all of them were wearing JNA uniforms. There were many soldiers in the area. Some were saying: "They are not animals," things like that. One of them said: "You, and you," talking to my brother, and I thought that would be the end of it. But they wanted us to carry a person on a stretcher. This man was apparently from Keraterm. His body was emaciated. He was very thin. I don't know what happened to him later on. When we reached our territory, we handed him over to our men. I don't know what happened to him later on, whether he survived or not. So that's how it was. Later on, I joined the 1st Krajina Brigade, and after two months, I left to Croatia. Maybe a month later, actually.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: So for one or two months, you served in the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN KARAGIC
utterances.text: I did, at that time, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: You mentioned seeing a skeleton at your uncle's house. Where was your uncle's house?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN KARAGIC
utterances.text: In the area of Sredice. I don't think you can see it on this map.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would another map which I would like. I don't believe it has been used before. It is labelled "Brdo region, Prijedor" and has the ERN number of 02166225.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Provisional S169. Okay, 170.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: If it can be shown to the witness, put on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Sir, I'd like you to look at the map, and first, if you can find your village, Rizvanovici.

utterances.speaker: NERMIN KARAGIC
utterances.text: This is where the house of my uncle was, approximately. This whole area is the area of Rizvanovici.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Okay. The witness has indicated for the record just to the north-east of Rizvanovici and just lightly north-west of Duratovici.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: You also talked about being arrested at Duratovici.

utterances.speaker: NERMIN KARAGIC
utterances.text: Duratovici also forms part of Rizvanovici. It's just a hamlet, the name of the hamlet.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you. And you also see the place where you were arrested, Rakovcani?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN KARAGIC
utterances.text: Yes, here.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Can you show us where -- from your house, you said you were able to see the shelling of Hambarine. Can you show us where Hambarine is?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN KARAGIC
utterances.text: Here. This whole area here is the area of Hambarine. This is the main road for Ljubija. This whole area here is called Hambarine. It stretches over 2 and-a-half kilometres in the direction of Rakovcani. It has about 800 houses. That's what people tell. I don't know personally. Hambarine is the largest village in the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: For the record, the witness indicated the road above Hambarine on the map and indicated the area to the east towards Tukovi.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Do you see where the convoy was that you -- where you boarded the convoy on the 21st of August?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN KARAGIC
utterances.text: I think that it could be here. This whole area is Tukovi. If this is the road for Rizvanovici, then it would be here.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Indicating the area marked Tukovi and the area to the north-east of that. Thank you. Sir, in addition to your uncle, did you lose any other relatives during the conflict in 1992? In addition to your uncle and your father, excuse me.

utterances.speaker: NERMIN KARAGIC
utterances.text: I lost another uncle, three cousins, sons of my uncle, that is, my father's brother. And then I lost also two cousins of my mother's brother. And then, of course, my father. I'm not going to enumerate all of my relatives who got killed because so many people from this area got killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Do you know if your house was ever looted?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN KARAGIC
utterances.text: When?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: That was going to be my next question. Was your house looted, to your knowledge? And if you know, when did that occur?

utterances.speaker: NERMIN KARAGIC
utterances.text: Well, in the days that followed the cleansing, we knew about it, all of the valuable things were taken away immediately after that, such as the TV set, the tractor. So yes, I am aware of that, of the fact that it was looted as early as then. Other things were taken later on. But the most valuable property was taken right away. They were fighting for it. Though, I know, for instance, that my uncle's combine, I know where it is. But my uncle has no way of proving that it is his combine. He has no documentation to that effect. I don't think he will succeed in recovering it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you, sir, for your information.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: I don't have any further questions on direct examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: May I ask the Defence counsel, is it your intention to cross-examine the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. We would have to clarify a few points.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: You need, of course, more than the remaining 20 minutes. Right?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, of course, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Then for today, the witness is excused. And may we ask you to come again tomorrow. There are some additional questions in the same manner as we did it today. Thank you for today. And we proceed a little bit --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I forgot to say something. So when I am asked further questions, I may remember to add those. I think you should know this in advance, some things I forgot to say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. We will come back to these issues tomorrow. Thank you for today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: There were two documents tendered today, the first map Ljubija, Brisevo overview. Objections?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: No objections, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: As regards the second, Brdo region, Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: No objections, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Then these two documents are admitted into evidence as S169, S170. Then can we hear from the Office of the Prosecutor what will be the next -- what can we expect as to the next witnesses to come, and what Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. about our missing witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: The witness who is in the middle of cross-examination, my understanding is he is scheduled to return the 1st of July, to be examined the 1st of July, which is Monday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Monday afternoon. And tomorrow, the cross-examination of the witness before us. And then?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: That's all that we had scheduled, would be the cross-examination and Judges' questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Yes. Then it may be necessary to add a Status Conference tomorrow. As regards the other witness, we have to go for a moment into closed session. Closed session, please.
